title: Energy costs shut European mills as North European coil rises to €770 a tonne
intro: Europe's steel industry dominates today's edition. Several publishers report that high energy costs are forcing output cuts, with kalkine.co.uk saying North European coil rose €10 to €770 a tonne as mills shut and import quotas ran out. ChemAnalyst reports widespread wire rod halts in Italy. On trade, France's President Macron has urged WTO action over US steel tariffs, according to Yeni Safak English, while the UK moves to mandate melt-and-pour declarations for imports. In the United States, Nikkei Asia reports a tentative labour pact at U.S. Steel, including a 19.25% wage rise over 4 years. POSCO's review of an Australian iron project and Meta's green steel arrangement with Stegra complete the picture. Much of today's material consists of headlines only, and we say so where it does.

marketOverview: Price data in today's material is sparse. The one firm figure comes from kalkine.co.uk, which reports that North European steel coil rose €10 to €770 a tonne. The publisher attributes the rise to energy-related mill shutdowns and exhausted import quotas. Металлургпром reports that northern European coil prices have risen but that Italian buyers are rejecting the new levels. It gives no figures. In Asia, BigGo Finance says China Steel and Chung Hung Steel raised December prices for a third straight month, without stating amounts. Shanghai Metals Market published its iron ore index for 19th November 2026 and a coking coal brief, but the excerpts give no price levels. SMM puts coke inventory at coking enterprises at 273,000 mt this week.

sections.title: China
sections.summary: BigGo Finance reports that China Steel and Chung Hung Steel have raised December prices for a third consecutive month, with mill margins expected to widen. Neither the size of the increases nor the products are given. Shanghai Metals Market reports that coke inventory at coking enterprises was 273,000 mt this week. It also published its iron ore index and coking coal brief, though without price detail. Separately, electrive.com reports that POSCO has won a major lithium order from CATL.

analysis: Analysis: Today's reports suggest that European steel is being squeezed from two directions. Energy costs appear to be forcing capacity offline, while trade defences tighten the supply of imports. If import quotas are indeed running out, as kalkine.co.uk's headline indicates, domestic mills could gain pricing power even as their own costs rise. The reported resistance from Italian buyers suggests that the ability to pass on those costs may vary by region. Producers seeking surcharges could test how much buyers will bear. On trade, Macron's call for WTO action, the UK's melt-and-pour rule and the EU's Vietnamese measure point to a more fragmented, rules-heavy market. Fastmarkets' report on Canadian regionalisation fits the same pattern. In decarbonisation, POSCO's cautious language on its Australian HBI project, the Stegra-Meta arrangement and calls for CBAM clarity together suggest that investment is moving forward but remains contingent on policy certainty. These links are interpretive: the material provided is mostly headlines and does not quantify any of these effects.
